lessons.title: Gates, Frames and Doors
lessons.body: Aluminium gates, frames, and doors are in high demand across Africa because they resist rust, look modern, and last for years. To build a standard pedestrian gate, you need 40x40mm square tube for the frame, 25x25mm for the infill, and 2mm thick aluminium sheet for panels. Start by measuring the opening: a typical gate is 1m wide and 1.8m high. Cut your tubes with a mitre saw or a hacksaw with a mitre box, ensuring 45-degree corners for a clean join. Clean the cut ends with a stainless steel wire brush, then clamp the pieces on a flat welding table. Use a TIG welder with 2% thoriated tungsten electrode and 4043 filler rod (1.6mm diameter). Set the machine to 80-100 amps for 2mm thickness. Weld tack welds at each corner first, check for square by measuring diagonals, then weld the full joints. For doors, use 50x50mm frame with 3mm thickness; increase amps to 120-140. Add hinges by drilling and tapping, or weld pre-made steel hinges if you use a bi-metal insert. For frames around windows, use 40x40mm and weld at 90 degrees; a corner bracket helps alignment. Always wear a welding helmet with shade 10-12, leather gloves, and a respiratorâaluminium fumes are harmful. After welding, grind smooth with a flap disc, then finish with a wire brush and apply a clear lacquer or powder coat. A simple gate takes 2-3 hours and can sell for $150-$300 depending on design. Start with a small gate for a neighbour, then scale up.

lessons.title: Aluminium Boats and Canoes
lessons.body: Aluminium boats are ideal for African lakes, rivers, and coastal waters because they are lightweight, don't rot, and need less maintenance than wood. A typical 4-meter canoe or small fishing boat uses 3mm thick marine-grade aluminium sheets (5052 or 5083 alloy) for the hull and 40x40mm square tube for the gunwales and ribs. You will need a TIG welder capable of 200 amps, 5356 filler rod (1.6mm or 2.4mm), and a spool gun for MIG if you prefer faster welding on thicker sections. Start by building a jig from timber or steel to hold the hull shape. Cut the bottom sheet to size, then bend the sides using a brake or by clamping between two strong boards and hammering gently. Tack weld the hull seams every 100mm, then weld continuously with a slight back-step technique to control distortion. Use a heat sink (a copper bar) behind the seam to prevent burn-through. For ribs, space them every 400mm along the length. Weld the gunwales on top, then add a transom for an outboard motor using 6mm plate. Test for leaks by filling with water before painting. A 4m boat takes about 40-60 hours to build and can sell for $1,500-$3,000. Safety: always work in a well-ventilated area, and wear a P100 respirator when welding aluminium. Start with a small 2.5m dinghy to learn the techniques.

lessons.title: Water Tanks and Containers
lessons.body: Aluminium water tanks are popular in rural Africa because they are lighter than concrete, don't rust like steel, and can be repaired easily. A typical 1000-litre tank is made from 3mm aluminium sheet rolled into a cylinder, with a 4mm bottom and top. You need a sheet roller or a local metal fabricator to roll the body. Cut the sheet to size: for a 1m diameter and 1.3m height, the circumference is 3.14m, so cut 3.2m to allow overlap. Weld the vertical seam using TIG with 4043 filler at 120-140 amps, using a back-step to reduce distortion. Then weld the bottom plate to the cylinder with a fillet weld, and add a top with a manhole cover. Reinforce the tank with two 25x25mm angle rings around the circumference, welded at 200mm intervals. For containers like jerry cans or small drums, use 2mm sheet and a MIG welder with 1.2mm wire for speed. Always pressure-test the tank by filling with water and checking for leaks; mark leaks and re-weld after draining. A 1000L tank takes about 8-10 hours to build and sells for $200-$400. For food-grade containers, use 5052 alloy and clean welds with a stainless brush, then passivate with nitric acid paste. Safety: aluminium dust is explosive, so keep the work area clean and use a fume extractor.

lessons.title: Truck Bodies and Trailers
lessons.body: Aluminium truck bodies and trailers are big business in Africa because they are lighter than steel, which saves fuel and increases payload. A typical truck body for a 7-tonne truck uses 2mm corrugated aluminium sheet for the sides and 3mm for the floor, with a frame made from 60x60mm square tube. You will need a MIG welder with a spool gun (200-250 amps) because TIG is too slow for long seams. Use 5356 filler wire (1.2mm). Start by building the base frame on a flat concrete slab, ensuring it is square by measuring diagonals. Weld the crossmembers every 500mm. Then attach the floor sheet with plug welds every 150mm, followed by seam welds. For the sides, weld the corrugated panels to the vertical posts, using a stitch weld (50mm weld, 100mm gap) to control distortion. Add a front bulkhead and a tailgate with hinges and latches. For trailers, build a chassis from 100x50mm rectangular tube, then add a deck and sides. A 6-meter trailer takes 60-80 hours and sells for $3,000-$6,000. Always use a jig or clamps to keep everything aligned. Safety: use a welding curtain to protect bystanders, and wear a leather apron. Start with a small utility trailer to learn the skills.

lessons.title: Signs and Structures
lessons.body: Aluminium signs and structural frames are everywhere in African citiesâfrom shop signs to billboard supports and bus shelters. For a typical 2m x 1m sign, use a 40x40mm frame with 2mm aluminium composite panel (ACP) or 3mm sheet. Weld the frame with TIG at 90-110 amps using 4043 filler. For the face, you can weld on a 1mm aluminium sheet or use self-tapping screws if the sign is removable. For large billboards, build a truss structure from 50x50mm tube with diagonal bracing, welded at 120 amps. For bus shelters, use 80x80mm posts and a roof frame from 40x40mm, with polycarbonate sheets attached. Always check for wind loads: in coastal areas, use thicker material and more bracing. Weld all joints fully to prevent water entry. After welding, grind smooth and paint with zinc-rich primer and topcoat. A simple shop sign takes 2-3 hours and sells for $50-$150; a bus shelter takes 20-30 hours and sells for $800-$1,500. Safety: when welding overhead, wear a leather cape and use a fire blanket. Start with small sign frames for local shops, then move to larger structures.

lessons.title: Repair Work: The Steady Income
lessons.body: Repair work is the bread and butter of an aluminium welder in Africa because everything from pots to truck bodies gets damaged and needs fixing. Common repairs include cracked water tanks, broken gate hinges, leaking boat seams, and torn truck sides. For a cracked tank, drain it, clean the area with a stainless brush, and grind a V-groove along the crack. Weld with TIG using 4043 filler at 100-120 amps, starting from the crack ends and working inward. For a broken hinge on a gate, cut off the old hinge, clean the area, and weld a new one with 4043 filler at 90 amps. For boat seams, re-weld with 5356 filler after cleaning with acetone. For truck body tears, use a MIG spool gun with 5356 wire at 180-200 amps, and add a backing plate if the tear is large. Always test your repair: fill tanks with water, open and close gates, and check boats in water. Charge by the hour or by the job: a small repair $10-$30, a large one $50-$200. Keep a portable welder and a generator for on-site repairsâmany customers will pay extra for you to come to them. Safety: always disconnect power before repairing electrical components, and wear a respirator when welding dirty aluminium. Build a reputation for quick, reliable repairs, and you will never lack work.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Real Products, Real Money

In aluminium welding, the difference between a workshop that survives and one that thrives is rarely the welding machine. It is the product mix. A welder who can only repair a cracked chair earns repair money. A welder who can build a gate, a boat, a water tank, a truck body, a sign frame, and then repair all of them earns product money, project money, and repeat maintenance money.

This Practical Reference module pulls together the six product families in this course â gates, frames and doors; boats and canoes; water tanks and containers; truck bodies and trailers; signs and structures; and repair work â into one working document. Use it as a bench reference, a pricing prompt, and a sales tool. The numbers are indicative for a small to medium aluminium fabrication workshop in sub-Saharan Africa, and they must be adjusted for your local metal prices, labour rates, transport, and taxes.

Why Product Mix Beats Single-Product Shops

Aluminium is expensive relative to mild steel, so the business case for aluminium rests on three advantages: it does not rust, it is light, and it can be extruded into profiles that assemble quickly. That means aluminium wins where corrosion, weight, or assembly speed matter â coastal towns, truck fleets, water storage, signage, and marine work. A workshop that understands this can charge a premium for lifespan and low maintenance, not just for labour.

In practice, a healthy African aluminium workshop runs a portfolio: fast-turnaround repair jobs to cover daily costs, medium-ticket products (gates, frames, signs, tanks) to build margin, and larger project work (boats, truck bodies, trailers) to build reputation and cash reserves. The six lessons in this module are the six revenue streams. The skill is in sequencing them so that cash from repairs funds materials for products, and product profits fund the tooling and certification needed for bigger projects.

Line 1: Gates, Frames and Doors

This is the entry product line for most aluminium workshops because it needs only a mitre saw, a TIG or MIG set, and a flat assembly table. Aluminium gates and window frames sell on corrosion resistance and low weight. In coastal cities such as Mombasa, Dar es Salaam, Lagos, and Accra, salt air destroys steel gates within a few years, while aluminium frames can last decades with minimal maintenance.

Key commercial points: standardise your profiles so you buy in bulk; keep a small catalogue of gate and frame designs with fixed prices; and offer installation as a separate line item. Frames are often sold to builders in batches, so a relationship with two or three contractors can keep a workshop busy for months.

Line 2: Aluminium Boats and Canoes

Aluminium boats are a natural fit for Africa's lakes, rivers, and coastlines. They are lighter than steel or timber, do not rot, and need less maintenance. The market includes fishing canoes, passenger boats, patrol and rescue craft, and small cargo boats. This is higher-risk work because a failed hull weld is a safety failure, so only welders with solid TIG/MIG experience and proper jigs should take on hull fabrication.

Business notes: boats are usually sold on specification, not on a shelf, so you need a written design, a deposit, and a clear delivery date. Partner with a naval architect or an experienced boat builder for your first few hulls. Marine-grade 5083 or 6061 alloys are preferred; never substitute a general-purpose alloy in a hull without engineering advice.

Line 3: Water Tanks and Containers

Aluminium water tanks are popular for rooftops, farms, and construction sites because they are lighter than concrete or steel and resist corrosion. Typical products are rectangular or cylindrical tanks, transport containers, and food-grade bins. Welding quality is critical: any pinhole leak wastes water and destroys your reputation. Pressure-test every tank before delivery.

Business notes: tanks are a volume product, so jigs and templates pay for themselves quickly. Offer a standard range of sizes with published prices, plus custom sizes at a premium. In dry regions, a tank is an essential purchase, not a luxury, which makes demand more resilient than gate or signage demand.

Line 4: Truck Bodies and Trailers

Aluminium truck bodies and trailers are a high-value line. The weight saving over steel improves fuel economy and payload, which fleet owners understand. Typical work includes flatbed bodies, box bodies, tipper bodies, fuel tankers, and livestock trailers. This is project work: it requires drawings, jigs, lifting equipment, and often a second welder.

Business notes: fleet contracts are the prize. A single transport company can order ten bodies a year, plus repairs. Price by weight of metal plus fabrication hours plus a project margin. Always agree on axle ratings, load capacity, and inspection requirements in writing before cutting metal.

Line 5: Signs and Structures

Aluminium signage and light structures â billboard frames, shopfronts, canopies, stair rails, and display stands â are steady, visible work. Signage is often repeat business because businesses rebrand, expand, and repair. Aluminium is preferred for outdoor signs because it does not rust and takes paint or vinyl well.

Business notes: signage has short lead times and high margin per kilogram. Structures such as canopies and railings are more engineering-heavy and may need load calculations. Keep a portfolio of photographs; in this line, a visible finished sign is your best advertisement.

Line 6: Repair Work â The Steady Income

Repair work is the base of the pyramid. It pays daily wages, uses small amounts of material, and generates customer relationships that lead to product sales. Typical repairs include cracked frames, broken gate hinges, leaking tanks, damaged truck bodies, bent sign frames, and boat hull patches. Repair customers often become product customers.

Business notes: price repairs by a minimum call-out fee plus material plus labour, not by guesswork. Keep a repair log with customer names, phone numbers, and the work done. That log is a ready-made marketing list for your next product promotion.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Aluminium Welding Hazards

Aluminium welding produces intense ultraviolet radiation, ozone, and fine metal fume. Always wear a properly rated auto-darkening welding helmet, flame-resistant clothing, leather gloves, and safety boots. Weld in a well-ventilated area or use fume extraction â never weld in a closed room. Aluminium dust from grinding and cutting is combustible; keep it away from sparks and clean it up daily. Never weld a sealed tank, drum, or container that has held fuel, chemicals, or unknown liquids â residual vapour can explode. Purge, fill with water, or have the container professionally cleaned and certified before any hot work. Cylinders must be secured upright, and acetylene must never be used at pressures above 15 psi. In boats and tanks, ensure adequate ventilation and a fire watch during and after welding.

Indicative Cost and Margin Benchmarks

The table below gives indicative figures for a small workshop in an African urban market. Treat them as a starting template, not as fixed prices. Metal prices, transport, and labour vary widely by country and city.

Table 1: Indicative product economics for a small aluminium workshop (USD, 2024 estimates)
Product line Typical unit Material cost Labour & overhead Selling price Gross margin

Aluminium boat / canoe5â7 m hull1,800â3,500900â1,8004,000â7,50020â30%
Water tank1,000 L tank180â32080â160380â65025â35%
Truck body / trailer1 flatbed body2,500â5,0001,200â2,5005,500â10,50018â28%
Signs & light structures1 billboard frame150â400100â250400â90030â45%
Repair work1 job5â6015â8030â18035â55%

Sources: Ranges synthesised from UNIDO light-engineering SME cost-structure guidance, ILO Small Enterprise Development training materials, and published African metal-fabrication market surveys (2023â2024). Localise before quoting.

Skill and Equipment Requirements by Line

Different product lines demand different skills and tooling. This table helps you decide what to invest in next and what to subcontract or decline.

Table 2: Capability matrix â what each product line requires
Product line Core welding process Key equipment Skill level Quality check
Gates, frames, doorsTIG or MIGMitre saw, assembly table, clampsIntermediateSquare, level, smooth finish
Boats & canoesTIG (AC/DC), MIGHull jig, rollers, marine alloysAdvancedWatertight, leak test, hull symmetry
Water tanksTIG or MIGSheet roller, jigs, pressure test kitIntermediatePressure/leak test, clean interior
Truck bodies & trailersMIG (spray), TIG for thin sectionsJigs, overhead crane, alignment toolsAdvancedDimensional check, load test
Signs & structuresTIG for visible joints, MIG for framesBender, shear, drill pressIntermediateFinish quality, straightness
Repair workTIG or MIG depending on partPortable welder, hand tools, grinderBasic to intermediateFunction restored, no new cracks

Sources: Compiled from AWS Welding Handbook process-selection guidance, ESAB and Lincoln Electric aluminium welding technical manuals, and African marine and transport fabrication practice notes.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Quote in writing. Every job â repair or product â gets a written spec, price, deposit, and delivery date before any metal is cut.
  2. Take a 50â70% deposit on product and project work to buy materials; never fund a customer's project from your own cash.
  3. Match the alloy to the job. Use marine-grade alloy for boats, food-grade or appropriate alloy for tanks, and standard structural alloy for gates and frames.
  4. Use jigs and templates. They cut labour time, improve repeatability, and let you train helpers faster.
  5. Test before delivery. Pressure-test tanks, leak-test hulls, and load-check trailers and truck bodies.
  6. Keep a repair log. Names, numbers, and jobs done become your product sales list.
  7. Control fume and fire. Ventilate, extract, and never weld sealed or fuel-contaminated containers.
  8. Reinvest in one capability at a time. Add a bender, a jig, or a second welder only when a product line is consistently profitable.

Further Reading

  • UNIDO â Industrial Skills and Light Engineering Publications (free reports on SME fabrication and value chains).
  • ILO â Employment-Intensive Investment and Small Enterprise Development (free training and business guides).
  • African Development Bank â Jobs for Youth in Africa (free skills and enterprise resources).
  • American Welding Society â Welding Handbook and Technical Publications (process and safety reference).
  • ESAB â Aluminium Welding Technical Guides (free practical welding guides).

Bottom line: In aluminium fabrication, the product lines are not separate businesses â they are one business with six doors. Repair work keeps the lights on. Gates, frames, signs, and tanks build margin. Boats, truck bodies, and trailers build reputation and scale. Master the fundamentals, quote honestly, weld safely, and let the mix work for you.

quiz.q: What is the typical amperage range for TIG welding 2mm aluminium square tube?
quiz.explanation: For 2mm aluminium, 80-100 amps provides sufficient heat for a clean weld without burn-through.

quiz.q: Which filler rod is commonly used for TIG welding aluminium gates?
quiz.explanation: 4043 filler is widely used for general aluminium welding because it flows well and reduces cracking.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a jig when building an aluminium boat?
options: A) To hold the hull shape during welding
B) To cool the metal faster
D) To mix the filler gas
quiz.explanation: A jig holds the hull in the correct shape and prevents distortion during welding.

quiz.q: Which alloy is recommended for marine-grade aluminium boats?
quiz.explanation: 5052 (or 5083) has excellent corrosion resistance and is ideal for marine environments.

quiz.q: What is the typical thickness of aluminium sheet for a 1000-litre water tank body?
quiz.explanation: 3mm sheet provides enough strength for a 1000L tank while remaining workable.

quiz.q: Why is a back-step welding technique used on aluminium tanks?
quiz.explanation: Back-step welding distributes heat more evenly, minimizing warping and distortion.

quiz.q: What type of welder is best for long seams on a truck body?
options: B) MIG welder with spool gun
quiz.explanation: MIG with a spool gun is faster and more suitable for long, thick aluminium seams.

quiz.q: What is the typical spacing for crossmembers on a truck body frame?
quiz.explanation: 500mm spacing provides adequate support for the floor without excessive weight.

quiz.q: Which filler wire is recommended for MIG welding truck bodies?
quiz.explanation: 5356 filler offers higher strength and better feedability in spool guns for truck applications.

quiz.q: What is a common material for the face of an aluminium sign?
quiz.explanation: ACP is lightweight, weather-resistant, and easy to attach to aluminium frames.

quiz.q: Why is wind load important when building a bus shelter?
options: A) It determines the welding current
B) It affects the structural bracing needed
C) It changes the filler rod type
D) It requires preheating the metal
quiz.explanation: Wind load dictates the thickness of materials and the amount of bracing to prevent collapse.

quiz.q: What should you do before welding a cracked water tank?
options: B) Drain and clean the area
D) Heat it with a torch
quiz.explanation: Draining and cleaning removes contaminants and prevents dangerous steam or fumes.

quiz.q: What is the first step when repairing a broken gate hinge?
options: A) Weld the hinge while attached
B) Cut off the old hinge and clean the area
quiz.explanation: Removing the old hinge allows proper cleaning and full weld penetration on the new hinge.

quiz.q: Which safety equipment is essential when TIG welding aluminium?
quiz.explanation: A shade 10-12 helmet protects eyes from the intense UV and infrared radiation of aluminium welding.

quiz.q: What is the typical selling price for a simple aluminium pedestrian gate?
quiz.explanation: A basic gate, depending on design and local market, typically sells for $150-$300.

quiz.q: How long does it take to build a 4-meter aluminium boat?
quiz.explanation: A 4m boat requires about 40-60 hours of skilled labour, including cutting, welding, and finishing.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a heat sink when welding thin aluminium?
options: A) To cool the filler rod
quiz.explanation: A heat sink (e.g., copper bar) absorbs excess heat, preventing the thin sheet from melting through.

quiz.q: Which gas is used for TIG welding aluminium?
quiz.explanation: Argon is the standard shielding gas for TIG welding aluminium due to its inert properties.

quiz.q: What is the recommended overlap when rolling a tank body from sheet?
quiz.explanation: A 50mm overlap provides enough material for a strong seam weld without excessive waste.

quiz.q: Why should you use a stainless steel wire brush on aluminium before welding?
quiz.explanation: Aluminium oxide melts at a much higher temperature than the base metal, so it must be removed to prevent inclusions.

quiz.q: What is the typical amperage for MIG welding 3mm aluminium truck body panels?
quiz.explanation: 180-200 amps provides good penetration and deposition rate for 3mm aluminium with a spool gun.

quiz.q: Which repair job is considered 'steady income' for an aluminium welder?
options: B) Repairing cracked tanks and gates
quiz.explanation: Repairs are frequent and recurring, providing a consistent flow of work and income.

quiz.q: What is a common defect in aluminium welds if the metal is not cleaned properly?
quiz.explanation: Porosity is caused by hydrogen from moisture or hydrocarbons on the unclean surface.

quiz.q: What is the typical thickness of aluminium sheet for a truck body side panel?
quiz.explanation: 2mm corrugated sheet is commonly used for truck sides to balance weight and strength.

quiz.q: Why is a spool gun used for MIG welding aluminium?
options: A) Aluminium wire is too soft for standard liners
B) It provides better gas coverage
quiz.explanation: Aluminium wire is soft and prone to birdnesting in standard liners, so a spool gun feeds it directly.

quiz.q: What is the recommended shade for a welding helmet when TIG welding aluminium?
quiz.explanation: Shade 10-12 protects against the high UV and infrared radiation emitted during aluminium TIG welding.

quiz.q: What is the typical selling price for a 1000-litre aluminium water tank?
quiz.explanation: A 1000L tank, depending on local market and finish, typically sells for $200-$400.

quiz.q: What should you do after welding a water tank to ensure it doesn't leak?
options: B) Fill with water and check for leaks
C) Heat it with a torch
quiz.explanation: Filling with water is a simple and effective way to detect leaks before delivery.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common structural project for an aluminium welder?
quiz.explanation: Bus shelters are built from aluminium frames and are a common structural project.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of aluminium over steel for truck bodies?
quiz.explanation: Aluminium is about one-third the weight of steel, allowing for greater payload and fuel savings.
